title: Estimators
intro: After this lesson you can tell a parameter from a statistic, find a point estimate, and decide whether an estimator is unbiased by comparing the average of many estimates with the true value.

moments.title: Unbiased estimator
moments.text: An estimator is unbiased if, on average, it neither overestimates nor underestimates the parameter.

moments.title: Parameter
moments.text: A numerical summary of a population. The two you will use most are $\mu$ and $p$.

moments.title: Statistic
moments.text: A numerical summary of a sample, such as $\bar x$ or $\hat p$.

moments.title: Estimator
moments.text: A statistic used to estimate a population parameter.

moments.title: Three steps to check for bias
moments.text: Identify the parameter, look at many sample estimates, then compare their average with the parameter.

moments.title: Brushing teeth, unbiased
moments.text: The true proportion is 70%. Samples near 71%, 68%, 72%, 67%, 70% and 73% average out close to 0.70.

moments.title: Brushing teeth, biased
moments.text: Samples of 43%, 32%, 48%, 31% and 29% average far below 70%, so the estimates are biased low.

moments.title: Point estimate
moments.text: One statistic that points toward the parameter. $\hat p$ is a point estimate of $p$.

moments.title: Which statistics are estimators
moments.text: $\hat p$ estimates $p$, $\bar x$ estimates $\mu$, and a sample median or range can estimate its population version.

moments.title: Later school start times
moments.text: 150 of 200 students support it, so $\hat p=0.75$ is the point estimate of $p$.

moments.title: Mean test score
moments.text: Scores 82, 90, 88, 94 and 86 give $\bar x=88$, a point estimate of $\mu$.

moments.title: Name the parameter and the statistic
moments.text: Read the problem: the parameter is the proportion of all students, the statistic is $\hat p$ from the sample of 150.

moments.title: Parameter or statistic?
moments.text: If it describes all of a population, it is a parameter. If it comes from a sample, it is a statistic.

moments.title: Average of estimates equals the truth
moments.text: True $p=0.40$ and five estimates average exactly 0.40, so the estimator is unbiased.

moments.title: Average of estimates is too high
moments.text: True $\mu=150$ but five estimates average 156, a sign of bias.

moments.title: Why a random sample can be used as an estimator
moments.text: Random selection avoids favoring one kind of customer, so $\hat p=0.73$ points toward $p$.

cards.name: Parameter
cards.text: Describes a whole population, such as $p$ or $\mu$. There is one true value.

cards.name: Statistic
cards.text: Describes a sample, such as $\hat p$ or $\bar x$. It changes from sample to sample.

cells: Average height of all NBA players
Average height of 50 randomly selected NBA players
Proportion of all households in Ohio with a pet
Proportion of 500 sampled households with a pet
Proportion of the 150 surveyed students who have a part-time job

cards.name: Unbiased
cards.text: The average of many estimates is very close to the parameter.

cards.name: Biased
cards.text: The average of many estimates is consistently above or below the parameter.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video says samples chosen at random "should be" unbiased. Be more exact: random selection removes the systematic over- or under-representation that causes bias, so the center of the sampling distribution of $\hat p$ is $p$. An unbiased estimator still gives a different value in every sample.

sections.title: Check an estimator and find a point estimate
sections.intro: To decide whether an estimator is unbiased, look at many estimates, never just one. A single sample can miss by chance.
steps: Identify the parameter you are estimating, with the population and variable in context.
Look at many sample estimates of that parameter.
Find the average of the estimates. Close to the parameter means unbiased. Consistently high or low means biased.

parts.label: Sample proportion
parts.text: Point estimate of $p$, the proportion of all students who support later start times.

parts.label: Sample mean
parts.text: Point estimate of $\mu$, the mean score of all students.

parts.label: Another proportion
parts.text: Point estimate of the proportion of all voters who support the school levy.

sections.title: Sampling distribution explorer
sections.intro: Press Take 1,000 samples. Each sample gives one $\hat p$, and the histogram stacks them. For a random sample the dashed line, the average of the $\hat p$ values, lands on the true $p$. Switch to Biased sample and it moves away from $p$, even with a large $n$.

stories.nut: About 17% of a large population is allergic to peanuts. Each sample is 140 randomly chosen people, and we record the proportion who are allergic.
stories.teeth: Suppose 70% of all kids brush their teeth every night. Each sample is 100 randomly chosen kids.
stories.fan: Same 70%, but the survey is shared only on a toothbrush fan page, so kids who brush nightly are 1.5 times as likely to be in the sample.

sections.title: Write it so it earns credit

traps.title: Treating a sample value as the parameter
traps.weak: $p=0.75$ is the proportion of students who support later start times.
traps.better: $\hat p=0.75$ is the sample proportion. It is a point estimate of $p$, the proportion of all students at the school who support later start times.

traps.title: Naming the parameter without the population
traps.weak: The parameter is the proportion with a part-time job.
traps.better: The parameter is $p$, the proportion of all students at the high school who have a part-time job. The statistic is $\hat p$ from the random sample of 150 students.

traps.title: Thinking unbiased means every sample is right
traps.weak: The estimator is unbiased, so our sample proportion must equal the population proportion.
traps.better: Unbiased means the sampling distribution of $\hat p$ is centered at $p$. Any one sample proportion still varies from $p$.

traps.title: Judging bias from a single sample
traps.weak: The sample mean was 158 and the true mean is 150, so the estimator is biased.
traps.better: One sample can miss by chance. The five estimates average 156, well above 150, so the estimates are consistently high and the estimator is biased.

traps.title: Why a random sample supports using $\hat p$
traps.better: Because the customers were randomly selected, the sample is not systematically weighted toward fans or critics, so $\hat p$ is an unbiased estimator of $p$. It will still vary from sample to sample.

questions.stem: A company knows that 62% of all 40,000 of its customers renewed a subscription. A manager randomly selects 300 customers and finds that 57% renewed. Which statement is correct?
opts: 0.62 is a statistic and 0.57 is a parameter
0.62 is a parameter and 0.57 is a statistic
Both are parameters because both describe renewals
Both are statistics because both are proportions
why: The parameter describes all customers, so 0.62 is the parameter.
0.62 describes the whole population and 0.57 describes the sample.
Only the value for all customers is a parameter.
A proportion is a statistic only when it comes from a sample.

questions.stem: The true proportion of voters who favor a measure is 0.52. Five random samples give sample proportions 0.50, 0.55, 0.49, 0.54 and 0.53. What do these estimates suggest?
opts: The estimator appears unbiased, because the average, 0.522, is very close to 0.52
The estimator is biased, because no sample proportion equals 0.52
The estimator is biased, because the average is greater than 0.52
The estimator is biased, because the sample proportions differ from each other
why: Estimates vary, but their average is within 0.002 of the parameter.
Samples are not expected to match $p$ exactly. Bias is about the average.
0.522 is greater than 0.52 by only 0.002, which is not a systematic miss.
Variation from sample to sample happens for every estimator, biased or not.

questions.stem: Which statement describes an unbiased estimator?
opts: Every sample statistic equals the parameter
The statistic does not change from sample to sample
The mean of the sampling distribution of the statistic equals the parameter
The statistic comes from a sample larger than 10% of the population
why: Unbiased does not mean every estimate is exact.
Statistics always vary from sample to sample.
The center of the sampling distribution is the parameter, so on average the estimator is right.
Sample size and the 10% condition are not part of the definition.

questions.stem: A survey of 250 teenagers finds that 190 support a later start to the school day. What is the point estimate of the proportion of all teenagers who support it?
why: 190 is a count, not a proportion.
0.24 is the proportion who do not support it.

sections.title: Write a full response
sections.prompt: A town official wants to estimate the proportion of the town's households that recycle. She selects a random sample of 180 households and finds that 117 recycle.
parts: (a) Identify the parameter and the statistic.

(c) The official later learns that the true proportion is 0.65. Five more random samples of 180 households give sample proportions 0.64, 0.69, 0.66, 0.62 and 0.65. Find the average and decide whether these results are consistent with an unbiased estimator.
(d) A second official surveyed only people at the recycling drop-off. Five samples of 180 gave 0.91, 0.88, 0.93, 0.90 and 0.89. Is this estimator biased? Explain the cause.
sample: (a) The parameter is $p$, the proportion of all households in the town that recycle. The statistic is $\hat p$, the proportion of the 180 sampled households that recycle.

(c) The average of the five estimates is $(0.64+0.69+0.66+0.62+0.65)/5=0.652$, which is very close to the true value 0.65. The estimates vary but center on $p$, so they are consistent with an unbiased estimator.

(d) The average is $(0.91+0.88+0.93+0.90+0.89)/5=0.902$, far above 0.65. The estimates are consistently too high, so the estimator is biased. People at the drop-off are more likely to recycle, so the sample over-represents recyclers.
checklist: (a) Parameter defined with the population and variable, and $\hat p$ named as the statistic
(c) Concludes the estimator appears unbiased, noting that individual estimates vary
(d) Concludes biased and names the cause, a sample taken only from recyclers
